basis: fire reveals quality of each work
note: Paul says the day exposes each person's work as fire tests its quality; it links the commentary's burning at the end to an evaluation of accumulated human work.

basis: work burned and its maker suffers loss, yet is saved
note: The commentary likens failed works to ash blown away; Paul says a person's work may be burned and suffer loss while the person is saved, distinguishing lost product from lost person.

basis: work burns and worker loses
note: If a person's work burns, that person suffers loss even though saved; the precise distinction between a life and its ruined product clarifies the commentary's garden consumed late in life.

basis: one plants, another waters, God gives growth
note: The commentary turns plants joined together into people who urge one another; Paul describes distinct workers planting and watering within one field, while God supplies the growth.

basis: planting and watering; growth from God
note: Paul assigns planting and watering to different workers while God causes growth; the commentary's rain-fed community of mutually contributing lives receives a concrete division of work.

basis: plowman and thresher hope to share the crop
note: The commentary says produce has a due and pasture nourishes animals; Paul interprets the crop law as giving field workers hope of sharing the harvest, making labor and entitlement explicit.

basis: flesh like grass; flower falls
note: The letter quotes human flesh as grass whose flower falls; it transposes the commentary's withering harvest to the brevity of human life.

basis: admonish, encourage, help, and be patient with all
note: The commentary's exception consists of people who urge one another to truth and patience; Paul specifies communal admonition, encouragement of the fainthearted, help for the weak, and patience toward all.

basis: mutual counsel and patience with the weak
note: Paul directs the community to admonish some, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone; this spells out the mutual exhortation and care for vulnerable members pictured by the commentary's connected plants.

basis: surplus answers another's lack
note: Paul asks that one community's present abundance supply another's need; this makes the commentary's mutually joined believers and harvest due a concrete exchange of resources.

basis: seed for sowing and a growing harvest of righteousness
note: The commentary joins good works to a crop image; Paul says God supplies seed and increases the harvest of righteousness, explicitly making ethical fruit the result.

basis: seed and bread; harvest of righteousness
note: God supplies seed and food and multiplies the harvest of righteousness for givers; the commentary's rain-fed grain and obligation to share meet in this single farming image.

basis: generous sowing yields a generous harvest
note: The commentary links righteous deeds and harvest; Paul applies sowing and reaping to generosity, making shared giving the deed that determines the yield.

basis: sowing generosity; proportional harvest
note: Paul's giving appeal says sparing and generous sowing have corresponding harvests; this adds the commentary's almsgiving setting to its agricultural account of human gain.

basis: distribution to poor as righteousness
note: In Paul's quotation, one who distributes to the poor has righteousness that endures; it explains how the commentary's crop right at harvest becomes a lasting moral yield.

basis: truth spoken as the body grows
note: The commentary's people mutually counsel one another to truth; Ephesians joins speaking truth with growing into Christ, adding growth as the outcome of truthful communal practice.

basis: truth spoken in love as growth
note: Speaking truth in love, believers grow toward Christ; this joins the commentary's charge to exhort in truth with its unusual image of shared living growth.

basis: joined body grows as each part works
note: The commentary makes mutual counsel into plants connected as one green pasture; Ephesians describes a body joined together with every part working so it grows and builds itself up, a specific social counterpart to interconnected growth.

basis: joined parts cause communal growth
note: The whole body is joined and held together, each part working so it grows in love; though anatomical rather than botanical, it develops the commentary's claim that the faithful sustain one another by being connected.

basis: do good especially to fellow believers
note: Immediately after the promised harvest for persistent good work, Paul directs good to all, especially the household of faith; it identifies the mutual beneficiaries of the commentary's patient moral crop.

basis: what is sown is reaped
note: Paul says a person reaps what he sows; the commentary's crop as the product of a life receives an explicit ethical harvest formula.

basis: sowing to flesh reaps corruption; sowing to Spirit reaps life
note: The commentary says humanity is in loss except those who do good; Paul assigns contrasting harvests to two ways of life, making the ethical distinction a direct sowing-and-reaping contrast.

basis: corrupt or enduring harvest
note: Sowing to the flesh yields corruption while sowing to the Spirit yields life; the two outcomes sharpen the commentary's distinction between a ruined yield and enduring good action.

basis: doing good reaped in due season
note: The commentary links righteous action and patience; Paul says not to tire of doing good because the harvest comes at its season if they do not give up, making the ethical crop analogy explicit.

basis: persist in good; harvest in time
note: Paul urges against growing weary in doing good because a harvest will come if one does not give up; it ties the commentary's patient mutual goodness to sustained crop growth.

basis: consider one another for good works
note: The community is to attend to one another so as to stir love and good works; this gives a specific ethical action beside the commentary's joined plants representing believers who mutually urge what is right.

basis: exhort one another each day before hardening
note: The addressees must encourage one another daily while it is called Today so no one hardens; the commentary's reciprocal exhortation and closing time horizon meet in a concrete repeated practice.

basis: rained land produces useful vegetation
note: The commentary's cloud gives rain and the exception is a green, productive community; Hebrews compares hearers to land that drinks frequent rain and produces useful vegetation, interpreting response as fruitful growth.

basis: rain drunk by earth; useful crop
note: The earth repeatedly drinks rain and grows useful vegetation for its cultivators; this matches the commentary's rain-to-productive-growth sequence and makes the crop's value depend on what it yields.

basis: thorns, curse, and burning
note: The commentary's storm can burn an entire garden; Hebrews contrasts productive land with ground bearing thorns and thistles, near a curse and destined for burning.

basis: thorns after rain; final burning
note: The same watered earth bears thorns and ends in burning; this supplies a direct reversal of the commentary's fruitful growth destroyed at the end.

basis: rich person fades like flower
note: James compares the rich person's passing to a wild flower; it joins the commentary's accumulated material yield with the brief life of vegetation.

basis: scorching heat withers pursuits
note: A rising sun with scorching heat dries the grass and drops its flower, as the wealthy fade amid their pursuits; this is another sudden destruction of apparent prosperity.

basis: rain yields earth's fruit
note: Elijah prays again, heaven gives rain, and earth produces its fruit; this explicitly joins the commentary's rain cloud to its eventual productive crop in a communal prayer setting.

basis: unpaid harvesters' wages cry out
note: The withheld wages of harvest workers cry to the Lord in James's indictment of wealthy landowners; it gives the commentary's harvest due an economic and ethical edge.

basis: fattened hearts on day of slaughter
note: James says unjust rich people have fattened their hearts in a day of slaughter, immediately after the unpaid harvesters' cry; it gives the commentary's spring fatness an ominous late reckoning tied to harvest injustice.

basis: farmer waits for fruit and early and late rain
note: The commentary connects rain-fed growth with patience; James tells believers to wait like a farmer for the earth's precious fruit through the rains, adding patient expectation to the crop image.

basis: farmer waits for fruit and rains
note: James urges patience by the farmer waiting for the precious crop and its early and late rains; the commentary's rain-grown yield is joined here to the explicit virtue of patient endurance.

basis: community told to be patient and strengthen hearts
note: The commentary says the righteous mutually urge one another to patience; James addresses the community and tells them to be patient and steady-hearted as the Lord's coming draws near.

basis: grain dies and bears much fruit
note: The commentary's late-life storm destroys a life's yield; Jesus says a grain of wheat that dies produces much fruit, turning the death of a seed into multiplication rather than loss.

basis: dying grain produces many seeds
note: A wheat grain must fall and die to bear much fruit; it is an inverse agricultural path to the commentary's mature garden destroyed at the end, with the loss occurring before abundance rather than after it.

basis: fruitless branches removed; fruitful branches tended
note: Jesus distinguishes a branch removed for bearing no fruit from one pruned to bear more; this adds the maintenance of living, productive attachment to the commentary's plants joined together.

basis: branch joined to vine bears fruit
note: Jesus says a branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine; this directly illuminates the commentary's unusual image of plants joined together as the condition of living growth.

basis: vine and branches bear fruit by remaining joined
note: The commentary says those excepted from loss interconnect like continuous greenery; Jesus depicts branches joined to a vine and bearing much fruit by abiding, giving the joined-plant image a communal source of fruitfulness.

basis: abiding together yields abundant fruit
note: The vine and branches produce much fruit through remaining joined; it supplies a relational image for the commentary's exception of people who sustain one another like contiguous plants.

basis: severed branch withers and is burned
note: The commentary's crop can be destroyed by a fiery whirlwind; Jesus says the branch that does not abide withers, is gathered, and burned, joining disconnection, loss, and fire.

basis: severed branch withers and burns
note: A branch that does not remain is cast out, dries, is gathered, and burns; it states the exact contrary fate of the commentary's joined vegetation and burning garden.

basis: reaper gathers fruit for life and sower and reaper rejoice together
note: The commentary pictures a community made fruitful through linked action; Jesus describes harvest workers rejoicing together as fruit is gathered, giving shared labor and shared outcome a concrete scene.

basis: one sows while another reaps
note: The commentary connects mutual exhortation with plants joined into continuous growth; Jesus' saying assigns sowing and reaping to different people, making cooperation across roles explicit.

basis: reaping what others labored to sow
note: The commentary's green community is formed through reciprocal action; Jesus says his hearers enter work others began, adding continuity across generations of sowers and reapers.

basis: abundant land produce
note: Jesus begins the rich fool's story with land yielding abundantly; this supplies the productive first stage of the commentary's lifetime crop lost near its end.

basis: abundant crops stored in larger barns
note: The commentary's harvest can represent a life's accumulated product; the rich man plans larger barns for his abundant produce, making stored yield the object later put at risk.

basis: new barns for gathered harvest
note: The man plans larger barns to store grain and goods; his amassed agricultural gain is the counterpart of the commentary's stacked food and accumulated life's produce.

basis: stored crop seems to promise many years
note: The rich farmer addresses his soul as if stored goods guarantee years of ease; this expectation makes the next verse's sudden end a sharper counterpart to the commentary's late loss of a life's product.

basis: life required before stored goods can be used
note: The commentary says the storm may destroy the whole accumulation late in life; the rich man is told that his life is required that night and is asked who will own his stored goods, making the harvest's futility personal.

basis: life ends before harvest can secure him
note: God demands the man's life that night and asks who will own his stores; the reversal mirrors the commentary's late catastrophe that makes an accumulated yield useless.

basis: fig tree given another year and extra care
note: The commentary joins patience to the crop's fate; the gardener asks for another year to dig and fertilize a fruitless fig tree, making patience an intervention that could change the harvest.

basis: last season to make fig tree fruitful
note: The gardener asks for one more year to tend the fruitless fig tree; this creates a patient interval before the kind of final crop judgment the commentary describes.

basis: fruit determines whether the tree is spared or cut down
note: The commentary contrasts productive greenery with crop loss; the gardener's final condition is that the tree bear fruit or be cut down, making the outcome hinge on yield.

basis: fruit or cutting down
note: If the tree bears after tending it may remain, otherwise it will be cut down; the commentary's survival of fruitful growth and loss of an unproductive garden meet in this conditional ending.

basis: growth choked before maturity
note: Jesus says the seed crowded by cares, riches, and pleasures never reaches mature fruit; it gives the commentary's threatened crop a specific failure of ripening through worldly entanglement.

basis: fruit borne with endurance
note: The commentary joins good deeds and patience to its crop imagery; Luke's good-soil hearers hold fast and bear fruit with endurance, directly linking ethical reception to patient yield.

basis: fruit borne with patience
note: Jesus describes good soil bearing fruit with perseverance after receiving the word; the commentary's patient, connected greenery becomes a specific figure for enduring faithful people.

basis: seed on bare rock withers for lack of moisture
note: Seed on rock sprouts but dries because it has no moisture; the commentary's hard bare stone is a precise contrary surface to its watered, continuous greenery.

basis: seed scattered on the ground
note: The commentary follows rain through plant growth to harvest; Jesus begins a kingdom parable with a person scattering seed, adding the human act that starts the growth sequence.

basis: seed grows while the sower does not know how
note: The commentary makes the rain-fed growth of plants an image for a community's flourishing; in Jesus' parable the earth produces growth beyond the sower's understanding, adding the hidden process between sowing and harvest.

basis: stalk, head, then full grain
note: The commentary says the grain is named عصر when its husk appears and then describes its yield; Mark's seed parable traces growth through stalk, head, and full grain, closely matching that crop-stage sequence.

basis: blade then ear then full grain
note: Jesus describes the earth producing first a blade, then an ear, then full grain in the ear; the commentary's distinctive attention to visible grain husks and mature crop finds a staged analogue.

basis: sickle when the harvest is ready
note: The commentary moves from grain's formation to its yield; Mark ends the growing sequence with the sickle at harvest, supplying the moment when the crop becomes gathered produce.

basis: harvest when grain permits
note: When the grain is ripe, the sower sends the sickle because harvest has come; it provides the decisive harvest moment beside the commentary's produce and harvest-day obligation.

basis: wealth chokes growing seed
note: In Jesus' explanation, wealth's deceit chokes the word so it becomes unfruitful; it offers an ethical counterpart to the commentary's showy spending and lost crop.

basis: good soil yields manyfold
note: The receptive person is good soil that bears a multiplied crop; the commentary's exceptional believers likewise appear as productive ground after the warning of loss.

basis: weeds burned while wheat is gathered
note: The commentary distinguishes the fruitful exception from a lost harvest; Jesus' harvest separates wheat for storage from weeds for burning, adding a final sorting of productive and useless growth.

basis: weeds burned, wheat stored
note: At harvest the weeds are bundled for burning while wheat is gathered into a barn; this places the commentary's stored grain and final fire at one decisive sorting, though its garden fire acts on an already productive plot.

basis: fruit season brings a claim on vineyard yield
note: At harvest time the vineyard owner sends servants to receive its fruit; this is a narrative counterpart to the commentary's assertion that fruit carries a due claim when harvested.

basis: community judged by fruit produced
note: Jesus says the kingdom will be given to a people producing its fruits; it parallels the commentary's exception of a faithful group pictured as an ongoing productive planting.

basis: grain gathered, chaff burned
note: The coming figure gathers wheat into the barn and burns chaff; it juxtaposes stored harvest with final fire, though the commentary's fire consumes a whole garden rather than separated chaff.

basis: rain falls on just and unjust alike
note: The commentary's cloud releases rain onto a community while its later image distinguishes the righteous exception; Jesus says rain falls on both just and unjust, adding an account of weather as an indiscriminate gift.

basis: showy alms seek human praise
note: Jesus warns against giving alms publicly for praise, because such givers have received their reward already; it directly illuminates the commentary's showy spending that yields no lasting benefit.

basis: birds fed without barns
note: Birds neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, yet God feeds them; the commentary's stores of grain and pasture for animals meet a different account of secure provision.

basis: grass lives today, burns tomorrow
note: Grass now growing in the field is soon thrown into an oven; the commentary's green abundance suddenly consumed by fire gains a short-lived plant counterpart.

basis: secret giving receives divine reward
note: Jesus says giving unseen by others is seen and repaid by the Father; it supplies the positive alternative to the commentary's showy donor whose apparent good is stripped away.

basis: unfruitful tree thrown into fire
note: A tree without good fruit is cut down and cast into fire; this relates the commentary's garden consumed by fire to a moral test of what the planting produced.

basis: rain and wind strike a house founded on rock, but it stands
note: The commentary pairs a destructive storm with hard stone; Jesus' house withstands rain, flood, and wind because it is founded on rock, making stability the opposite outcome of the ruined garden.

basis: rain and wind test true work
note: Rain, floods, and winds strike the house that survives because its builder acted on Jesus' words; this gives the commentary's storm a test of lived conduct rather than a mere weather event.

basis: rain and wind destroy failed work
note: The same storm makes the house of the hearer who does not act collapse; it parallels the commentary's image of a whole life's work lost in a violent final event.

basis: watered tree gives fruit every month
note: The tree of life stands by the river and yields fruit month after month, with leaves for the nations' healing; it offers the commentary's connected, uninterrupted greenery an enduring communal yield.

basis: strong wind strips unripe fig tree
note: Stars fall like unripe figs shaken from a fig tree by strong wind; the comparison gives the commentary's destructive wind a specific instance of fruit torn away before it can support anyone.

basis: hail and fire burn trees and green grass
note: The commentary's fire-bearing whirlwind burns a garden; Revelation's first trumpet sends hail and fire onto the earth, burning trees and green grass in an apocalyptic destruction scene.

basis: elm supports vine; vine yields fruit
note: Hermas sees a vine that bears abundant fruit by clinging to an elm that supports it; this is a particularly close Christian image for the commentary's plants physically joining so that growth can continue.

basis: rich supply poor; poor pray for rich
note: Hermas explains the elm and vine as materially generous rich people and poor people who pray for them; the joined plants thus yield reciprocal benefit, much as the commentary connects mutual support to the crop's due share.

basis: good deeds have fruit in this world and a principal kept for the next
note: The commentary exempts people who believe, do good, and counsel one another; Peah lists kindness and peacemaking among deeds whose fruit is enjoyed now while their principal remains for the world to come, giving the ethical exception a rabbinic account of reward.

basis: field corner and firstfruits as obligations
note: The Mishnah lists the field corner and firstfruits among duties with no fixed measure; it gives a Jewish legal setting for the commentary's claim that a crop carries a right owed to others at harvest.

basis: communal remembrance of rain at festival
note: The Mishnah debates when rain should first be invoked during the autumn festival; it places the commentary's rain-bearing cloud within a community's timed, recurring liturgical concern.

basis: prayed-for rain becomes destructive torrent
note: Honi asks first for rain, then for rain of favor when the downpour is too violent; the story distinguishes life-giving rain from a damaging storm within the commentary's weather sequence.

basis: continue the work without needing to finish it
note: The commentary's righteous community keeps urging patience while doing good; this maxim says one need not complete the work but is not free to desist, adding persistence when a lifetime may not see the yield.

basis: watered fruit tree and enduring shoots
note: The rabbinic blessing tells of a traveler nourished by a tree's fruit, shade, and water, then wishes its shoots to resemble it; it makes the commentary's productive greenery a source of care and continuity for later generations.

basis: flour and oil do not run out during drought
note: The commentary presents the harvest as lost; during a drought, the widow's flour and oil remain sufficient, a specific counterexample of provision continuing without a new crop.

basis: small cloud rising from the sea
note: The commentary develops rain-bearing clouds; Elijah's servant sees a cloud rising from the sea, a specific cloud sign that precedes the rain.

basis: small cloud rises before rain
note: Elijah's servant sees a small cloud rising from the sea after repeated inspection; the commentary's rain-bearing cloud gains a narrative moment before its release onto the land.

basis: sky blackens and heavy rain begins
note: The commentary moves from a rain cloud to the water it releases; after the small cloud, this verse describes darkening skies and heavy rain, completing that weather sequence.

basis: clouds, wind, and heavy rain
note: The sky darkens with clouds and wind and then heavy rain falls; this joins the commentary's cloud, forceful wind, and needed rainfall in a single scene following drought.

basis: عصر / עצר; table sound correspondence only; sky restrained
note: Solomon describes heaven shut so there is no rain when Israel sins; עצר names the restraint, contrasting with the commentary's cloud releasing water onto a community.

basis: عصر / עצר; table sound correspondence only; closed sky and eaten land
note: God says he can shut heaven against rain or send locusts to devour land; עצר makes a concrete opposite to the commentary's pressed rain cloud and fruitful harvest.

basis: communal repentance; land healed
note: If God's people turn and pray, he promises to heal their land; this adds a communal ethical remedy to the preceding rain-and-crop destruction and the commentary's collective exception.

basis: firstfruits grain given as food
note: A man brings firstfruits and fresh grain ears to Elisha, who orders them given to the people; the commentary's ears becoming food and a due share can be read beside this concrete communal distribution.

basis: mass of waters in thick clouds; חשר table sound match has different sense
note: David's hymn depicts God surrounded by dense water clouds; it supports the commentary's layered, water-filled cloud image on its own terms, while the table's חשר is semantically distinct from Arabic خسر 'loss'.

basis: rain allotted unequally to communities
note: God withholds rain from one city while another receives it, leaving one field watered and another dry; the commentary's cloud releasing rain upon a group becomes an ethical question of who receives it.

basis: blight destroys cultivated trees
note: God strikes gardens, vineyards, fig trees, and olive trees with blight and insects; this provides a more gradual counterpart to the commentary's storm destroying a developed crop.

basis: harvest overtakes planting
note: In promised restoration, the plowman catches the reaper and grape-treader the seed-sower; this is a striking instance of the commentary's continuous growth and yield with no gap between crops.

basis: plant vineyards and eat their garden fruit
note: Restored people plant vineyards and gardens and enjoy their fruit; it reverses the commentary's late disaster by letting the makers retain the mature garden's benefit.

basis: خسر / Aramaic חסר; table sound correspondence only; found deficient
note: Daniel declares the king weighed and found lacking; the Aramaic חסיר gives the commentary's loss an explicitly evaluated human life, though the consonant match alone does not prove cognacy.

basis: seasonal rain; gathered grain
note: The promised rains in their seasons allow Israel to gather grain, wine, and oil; this reproduces the commentary's move from rain cloud to usable produce.

basis: pasture for cattle; human satiety
note: God gives grass in the fields for livestock so that the people eat and are satisfied; it pairs the commentary's pasture feeding animals with the livelihood that follows.

basis: עצר; rain restrained (table sound correspondence only)
note: The commentary's ع ص ر image releases rain from a pressed cloud; the package's table gives Hebrew עצר as a sound correspondence, and this verse uses it for heaven being restrained so rain and land-yield cease.

basis: عصر / עצר; table sound correspondence only; rain shut off
note: The divine closing of the heavens stops rain and thus the land's produce; Hebrew עצר expresses restraint, a pointed reversal of the commentary's rain-releasing cloud and ensuing harvest.

basis: forgotten sheaf left for the vulnerable
note: The commentary says the crop has a due on harvest day; this law leaves a forgotten sheaf for the immigrant, orphan, and widow, showing harvested produce as a social obligation.

basis: forgotten sheaf belongs to vulnerable
note: A sheaf forgotten in the field is to remain for the foreigner, orphan, and widow; it specifies who receives the harvest's due, linking produce to the weak dependents in the commentary's garden scene.

basis: threshing ox allowed to eat grain
note: The commentary says pasture gives itself to the herd and the harvest has a due; this law lets the working ox eat from the grain it threshes, assigning a share of produce to the animal laborer.

basis: firstfruits presented before God
note: The commentary connects harvest to an owed share; this verse has the worshipper present the firstfruits as an offering, making the harvest's claim a liturgical act.

basis: rejoice with Levite and immigrant
note: The commentary makes fruitful life a shared community image; the firstfruits rite culminates in rejoicing with the Levite and immigrant, extending the crop's benefit beyond its grower.

basis: first produce placed in a basket
note: The commentary names the crop's due on harvest day; Deuteronomy requires the first of the land's produce to be gathered in a basket, giving that due a ritual form.

basis: sowing much, gathering little to locusts
note: The commentary's central loss image is a vanished harvest; this curse has abundant sowing yield little because locusts consume it, specifying one way the crop is lost.

basis: large sowing yields little because devoured
note: The people carry much seed to the field yet gather little because locusts consume it; this gives the commentary's human loss a specific crop-failure form within a covenant curse.

basis: vineyard work lost to infestation
note: They plant and tend vineyards but cannot drink the wine or gather grapes because worms consume them; it parallels the commentary's carefully built garden that fails to benefit its owner.

basis: מחסור; lack of everything (table sound correspondence only)
note: The commentary glosses خسر as a crop's disappearance; the package's חסר correspondence appears here in a covenant curse of hunger, thirst, nakedness, and total lack, making the loss material and collective.

basis: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; cultivated land without lack
note: In a land of abundant food, Israel will lack nothing, using Hebrew חסר; it is the explicit inverse of the commentary's crop as loss, with cognacy still only the table's unverified sound correspondence.

basis: full cloud empties rain on land
note: A cloud filled with water pours itself onto earth; this expresses the commentary's compressed rain cloud and its release without requiring a shared root.

basis: watching wind and clouds delays sowing and reaping
note: One who watches wind never sows and one who studies clouds never reaps; the commentary's cloud, wind, and crop are joined here to the danger that anxious waiting itself can forfeit harvest.

basis: sow morning and evening without slackening
note: The commentary's exception holds to patient good work; Ecclesiastes tells the sower not to rest because the successful yield is unknown, giving patience an agricultural practice.

basis: wealth perishes and son receives nothing
note: Ecclesiastes describes wealth lost through a bad venture and a son left with nothing; the combination of vanished lifetime gain and unprovided child closely matches the commentary's aged gardener and weak offspring.

basis: food shared without lack
note: Measured manna leaves neither surplus for the great gatherer nor lack for the small one; it offers an alternative to the commentary's stacked private food by meeting each person's need.

basis: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; no food deficit
note: The smaller manna gatherer does not lack, using חסר; the negated deficiency connects the commentary's loss to a shared-food scene that prevents it.

basis: east wind withers planted vine
note: Even a planted vine will wither when the east wind touches it; the commentary's productive garden similarly remains vulnerable to a destructive wind.

basis: vine spreads beside abundant water
note: The transplanted vine is set in good soil beside abundant water so it can bear branches and fruit; it parallels the commentary's rain-fed connected plants that grow into yield.

basis: fruitful vine by abundant waters
note: Ezekiel pictures a mother as a fruitful vine beside abundant water with many branches, paralleling the commentary's watered, connected vegetation as an image of a living group.

basis: east wind dries fruit; vine burned
note: Ezekiel's once fruitful vine is uprooted, dried by the east wind, and consumed by fire; the reversal closely matches the commentary's lifetime yield destroyed by a fiery storm.

basis: fire from vine consumes fruit
note: Fire emerging from the vine's own branch consumes its fruit and leaves no ruling branch; the commentary likewise reads the burned garden as a life's yield and vulnerable future lost together.

basis: fat flock tramples others' pasture
note: God rebukes those who feed on good pasture but trample the rest and muddy water for others; the commentary's pasture giving itself to animals meets a precise demand that abundance remain available to the weak.

basis: weaker flock inherits spoiled food and water
note: The other sheep must consume the trampled pasture and muddied water; this gives the commentary's vulnerable dependents a concrete counterpart harmed when the first beneficiaries misuse a shared meadow.

basis: judgment between fat and lean sheep
note: God judges between fat and lean sheep; this puts the commentary's fattened animal beside its concern for weak dependents and assigns moral weight to their unequal access to pasture.

basis: showers of blessing at the right season
note: God promises showers in their season for the restored flock; the commentary's cloud releasing rain upon a community becomes an explicit collective blessing.

basis: trees and land yield fruit after rain
note: The trees and ground yield produce and the people live secure after the promised showers; this completes the commentary's rain-to-harvest sequence with protection from loss.

basis: riverside trees fruit every month; leaves do not wither
note: The commentary's exception is continuous interconnected greenery; Ezekiel's riverbank trees never fail to fruit and keep healing leaves, extending the image to perennial abundance.

basis: no plants because no rain
note: Before the garden's plants had appeared, God had not yet caused rain on the earth; the negation makes rain the missing beginning of the commentary's sequence of growth.

basis: fat cows grazing beside lean cows
note: The commentary's camel fattens on spring growth; Pharaoh's dream makes fat, grazing cows the sign of abundant years, with their lean counterparts marking the coming reversal.

basis: صبر / צבר; table sound correspondence only; grain heaped
note: Joseph orders grain from the good years to be heaped and guarded against famine; Hebrew צבר matches the commentary's secondary صبر image of piled food, though the table's sound match does not establish etymology.

basis: stored harvest averts ruin
note: Joseph says the collected food will preserve the land through seven famine years; this offers a deliberate preservation of yield against the harvest loss envisaged in the commentary.

basis: צבר; grain heaped up (table sound correspondence only)
note: The commentary gives صبرة as food piled upon food; the package lists צבר as a sound correspondence, and Genesis uses it for Joseph's immense heaping of grain, matching the concrete heap sense.

basis: صبر / צבר; table sound correspondence only; piled grain
note: Joseph heaps grain in immense quantity before famine; the concrete stored-food heap corresponds to the commentary's صبرة of food stacked layer upon layer, without claiming proven cognacy.

basis: east wind blights grain ears
note: In Pharaoh's dream thin grain ears are scorched by the east wind; this gives the commentary's grain-ear stage a specific destructive counterpart before the harvest can feed anyone.

basis: thin ears swallow full ears
note: Seven thin ears consume the seven full ears in Pharaoh's dream; the image makes accumulated agricultural plenty disappear, as the commentary's late loss does.

basis: חק; a prescribed share of produce (table sound correspondence only)
note: The commentary calls the crop's due on harvest day its حق; the package's חקק correspondence means something prescribed, and Genesis fixes a fifth of the land's yield as a statute, making the crop's allotted share concrete.

basis: seedtime and harvest sustained
note: After the flood, God promises seedtime and harvest will continue while the earth remains; this stable cycle sets the ordinary expectation against which the commentary's ruined harvest is a reversal.

basis: heavens withhold dew; land yield
note: Because of the people's neglect, heaven withholds dew and earth withholds its produce; the commentary's rain, growth, and loss are compressed into one reversal.

basis: drought strikes grain and labor
note: The called drought reaches grain, wine, oil, people, animals, and all labor of hands; it relates a failed harvest to the whole community and its work, as the commentary does.

basis: much sowing; little gathered
note: Haggai lists much seed with little harvest and wages disappearing as if through a pierced purse; it connects the commentary's failed crop to the vanishing gain of human labor.

basis: expected harvest blown away
note: The people bring home little of what they expected and God blows it away; the image matches the commentary's wind-scattered works and abrupt removal of accumulated yield.

basis: sow righteousness; reap steadfast love; rain righteousness
note: The commentary joins good deeds and mutual counsel to its green-growth image; Hosea commands sowing righteousness and seeking God until rain comes, linking ethical action to a promised harvest.

basis: sow righteousness; reap mercy; awaited rain
note: Hosea calls the people to sow righteousness and reap loyal love until God comes and rains righteousness; it links the commentary's ethical injunction, patient waiting, rain, and harvest in one appeal.

basis: dew revives Israel's plant growth
note: God promises to be like dew to Israel, who blossoms and puts down roots; the commentary similarly treats renewed vegetation as a living people sustained by water.

basis: grain revives and vine blossoms
note: People return and flourish like grain and bloom like a vine; this gives the commentary's joined green community both its grain crop and vineyard forms.

basis: sowing wind, reaping whirlwind; stalk without a head yields no flour
note: The commentary's cyclone raises dust and its lost harvest disappears; Hosea binds whirlwind to failed grain, explicitly saying the stalk has no head and yields no flour.

basis: sow wind; reap whirlwind; grain without yield
note: Hosea makes wind sown into a whirlwind reaped, then says the stalk has no grain; it joins the commentary's storm, lost harvest, and failed human work in one agricultural judgment.

basis: chaff and dust before whirlwind
note: The nations' tumult is rebuked and chased like mountain chaff before wind and rolling dust before a storm; this shares the commentary's dust-raising whirlwind as an image of works unable to remain.

basis: whirlwind and devouring fire
note: Isaiah pairs whirlwind and tempest with the flame of a devouring fire in a judgment scene; it is a specific storm-and-fire analogue to the commentary's fiery whirlwind, though no crop is named in this verse.

basis: rain, abundant grain, and broad pasture
note: God promises rain for seed, rich grain from the land, and spacious pasture for livestock; the verse contains the commentary's sequence from cloud-water to crop and fed animals.

basis: fruitful field after outpouring
note: An outpouring from above transforms wilderness into a fruitful field; it gives the commentary's rain-to-garden movement a communal renewal sense.

basis: justice dwells in fruitful field
note: Justice comes to dwell in the transformed fruitful field; the commentary likewise places truth and a crop's due amid flourishing vegetation.

basis: grass and flower wither when wind blows
note: The commentary's cyclone lifts dust and destroys the crop; Isaiah says grass withers when the divine breath blows and identifies people with grass, bringing human transience into the weather image.

basis: grass withers at divine breath
note: Grass dries and flowers fall when God's breath blows on them; the commentary's wind-driven loss of lush vegetation likewise turns growth into impermanence.

basis: water on dry land and descendants
note: God promises to pour water on thirsty ground and blessing on descendants; the commentary's rain-fed greenery and concern for weak offspring meet through this joined promise.

basis: descendants grow like watered vegetation
note: Those descendants sprout like grass among watercourses; the verse makes a living group into adjacent flourishing plants, as the commentary does for the mutually supporting faithful.

basis: cultivated vineyard; failed fruit
note: The beloved prepares a vineyard and expects grapes but receives bad fruit; the text tests the commentary's claim that productive growth can figure the moral result of human work.

basis: fire consumes crop for rejected law
note: Fire consumes stubble and flame dries grass, while rotten roots and blown blossom picture those who rejected God's instruction; the commentary likewise lets a life crop end in fiery moral loss.

basis: vineyard exposed and trampled
note: The vineyard's hedge is removed so it can be devoured and trampled; its protection gives way to destruction, as the commentary's flourishing garden does at the end.

basis: rain withheld from ruined vineyard
note: God commands the clouds to give no rain to the now desolate vineyard; this reverses the commentary's rain-to-greenery sequence through judgment on a failed crop.

basis: fruit of justice expected
note: Isaiah identifies the vineyard as Israel and the expected crop as justice and righteousness, clarifying how the commentary's harvest imagery can evaluate human conduct rather than farming alone.

basis: rain makes earth sprout and yield seed and bread
note: The commentary moves from rain to plant growth and harvest; Isaiah's rain and snow water the earth so it sprouts, supplying seed for sowing and bread for food, a closely matched growth sequence.

basis: rain makes earth sprout, seed and bread
note: Rain and snow water the earth so it sprouts and gives seed and bread; the commentary's cloud, joined growth, grain, and food yield follow this same ordered sequence.

basis: feed the hungry and satisfy the afflicted
note: The commentary assigns the harvest a due and makes righteous action part of its green community; Isaiah makes feeding the hungry the condition of the promised light and renewal that follows.

basis: feed the hungry from one's own resources
note: Isaiah calls for giving sustenance to the hungry and meeting the afflicted person's need; this specifies an ethical use for the commentary's grain and its due share.

basis: watered garden and unfailing spring
note: The commentary joins righteous practice to a rain-fed green world; Isaiah promises that the person who acts for the hungry will be like a watered garden whose spring does not fail.

basis: giver becomes a watered garden
note: After the command to feed the hungry, the Lord promises the giver will be like a watered garden whose spring does not fail; this makes generous action itself the opposite of the commentary's garden destroyed after showy giving.

basis: garden makes righteousness sprout
note: As earth brings shoots forth and a garden grows what is sown, God makes righteousness and praise sprout before the nations; this makes the commentary's greenery a direct image of the good works expected from the saved group.

basis: plant vineyards and eat their fruit
note: The restored people plant vineyards and eat their own fruit; it is a direct positive inversion of the commentary's owner losing the garden that should have supported him.

basis: long-lived planters keep their yield
note: No one else will eat what the people plant, and their days are compared to a tree's days; this answers the commentary's late-life fear that an aged cultivator will lose his accumulated crop.

basis: no futile labor or children born for calamity
note: The people will not labor in vain or bear children for sudden disaster; both claims specifically reverse the commentary's burning garden and elderly owner with vulnerable offspring.

basis: watered tree endures heat and drought
note: The commentary's connected greenery stands against the lost harvest; Jeremiah's tree by water stays green in heat and continues bearing fruit even in drought, a specific image of endurance.

basis: rooted tree bears through drought
note: The person who trusts God is a tree rooted by water, remaining green through heat and bearing fruit in drought; this supplies a direct durable counterpart to the commentary's fruitful garden lost to adverse weather.

basis: grain, herd, and watered garden together
note: The restored people stream toward grain, wine, oil, young flock, and herd, becoming like a watered garden; one verse brings together the commentary's crop, pasture animals, and living garden community.

basis: rain and fixed harvest weeks
note: The people fail to acknowledge the giver of seasonal rain who preserves the appointed weeks of harvest; the verse makes rain and harvest an ordered provision with a moral obligation to recognize it.

basis: حق / חקק; table sound correspondence only; harvest ordinance
note: Jeremiah's fixed harvest weeks use חקות from the table's חקק family; the prescribed season provides a concrete counterpart to the commentary's conjunction of the crop and its due right, without equating the words.

basis: wrongdoing withholds good harvest
note: Jeremiah says sins have kept those good gifts from the people; the commentary's disappearance of yield likewise turns agricultural loss into a judgment on conduct.

basis: fatness and denied orphan's claim
note: Jeremiah calls prosperous people fat and sleek while they fail to defend an orphan's claim; it turns the commentary's image of fattening from abundant food toward the obligation to support vulnerable people.

basis: great wind collapses a house and kills the children inside
note: The commentary's fiery storm destroys a garden while its owner has weak children; Job's wind destroys a household and its children, adding the family cost of a sudden storm, though the objects and cause differ.

basis: wind kills children at life's height
note: A great wind strikes the house where Job's children are together and kills them; it offers a family-loss counterpart to the commentary's storm scene with vulnerable offspring, though Job's loss is not a garden fire.

basis: chaff swept by whirlwind
note: Job asks whether the wicked become chaff before wind and straw snatched by a whirlwind; the wording puts a human fate in the commentary's image of works scattered by a violent wind.

basis: water bound in clouds; cloud holds its burden
note: The commentary's cloud is compressed with rain before releasing it; Job depicts God binding water in clouds without their bursting, adding a precise image of cloud containment.

basis: waters bound inside cloud
note: God binds water within thick clouds without their bursting; this is a direct counterpart to the commentary's cloud filled with rain before releasing it.

basis: صبر / צבר; table sound correspondence only; piled wealth
note: The wicked man may heap silver like dust, yet the following verse gives it to others; צבר matches the commentary's piled store while the context makes accumulation vulnerable to loss.

basis: east wind carries away accumulated wealth
note: The east wind drives away the wicked person after the account of his piled silver; the commentary likewise makes wind undo accumulated gain.

basis: حق / חקק; table sound correspondence only; rain prescribed
note: God sets a prescribed order for rain; the Hebrew חק in a rain passage meets the commentary's rain sequence and its mention of a crop's due, while preserving the difference between ordinance and right.

basis: clouds pour rain on people
note: Job says the skies pour their drops abundantly upon humanity; the rain-laden cloud's release corresponds to the commentary's cloud giving water to a community.

basis: חשר; collection of watery clouds (table notes BDB's Arabic cognate)
note: The commentary develops rain-bearing and layered clouds, while the package's חשר entry describes a gathering of watery clouds and notes an Arabic cognate; Job's context concerns the spread of clouds, so the lexical link is suggestive but uncertain.

basis: cloud laden with moisture
note: Job describes a thick cloud burdened with moisture while its luminous cloud disperses; the burdened cloud resembles the commentary's rain-filled layers, but its release into a community is not explicit here.

basis: rain sent where no person lives
note: The commentary pictures rain delivered to a community; Job asks about rain given to an uninhabited land, adding the counterpoint that rain also serves places without human recipients.

basis: rain falls where no person lives
note: God sends rain even onto uninhabited desert land; it gives a specific counterpoint to the commentary's cloud raining upon a community, showing that the same gift can precede any human receiver.

basis: wilderness satisfied; grass sprouts
note: The commentary links rain with greening plants; Job's next verse says the desolate land is satisfied and tender grass sprouts, spelling out the water-to-growth result.

basis: desolate ground makes grass sprout
note: The rain satisfies waste ground and brings forth grass; this completes the preceding verse's empty-land rain with growth, extending the commentary's rain-to-pasture sequence beyond settled land.

basis: field ruined; grain destroyed
note: Joel's devastated land has ruined fields and grain, alongside dried wine and failing oil; it gives a specific prophetic instance of the commentary's harvest as loss.

basis: withered vine and joy
note: The vine and fig tree dry up, as do the other fruit trees, while human joy withers; it joins vegetative loss to lived human loss as in the commentary's ruined garden.

basis: fire devours pasture
note: Joel cries to God because fire has devoured the wilderness pastures and burned trees; it gives the commentary's animal-feeding meadow a destructive fiery counterpart.

basis: early rain and latter rain
note: The commentary links rain to plants that grow after it; Joel's restoration promise names seasonal rains as the setting for renewed agricultural abundance.

basis: restored seasonal rain
note: Joel promises early and later rain in restored measure; after the destroyed crop, this supplies a recovery of the commentary's rain-to-growth sequence.

basis: threshing floor full
note: After Joel's rain promise, this verse says the threshing floors fill with grain and vats overflow, giving the same rain-to-harvest sequence the commentary draws from cloud to crop.

basis: threshing floors fill with grain
note: The restored rains are followed by threshing floors filled with grain and vats with wine and oil; it gives a concrete positive answer to the commentary's lost and heaped harvest.

basis: vineyard gleanings for vulnerable
note: Grapes and fallen fruit must be left for the poor and resident alien; the harvest right extends to the commentary's vineyard and makes fruitfulness support others.

basis: harvest edge reserved for poor
note: The field's owner must leave the edge and gleanings at harvest; this gives an exact social practice beside the commentary's claim that a crop's right is given on harvest day.

basis: עצר; festival assembly (table's sound correspondence only)
note: The commentary describes rain falling on a community; the package's table pairs Arabic ع ص ر with Hebrew עצר and lists festival assembly as a Hebrew use, while Leviticus names an assembly at the ingathering festival. This is a lexical and communal echo, not proof of cognacy.

basis: spent labor yields neither crop nor fruit
note: The land will not give produce and the trees will not give fruit despite expended strength; the commentary's lost harvest is likewise the loss of a lifetime's labor, though this verse names no storm.

basis: seasonal rain and land's produce
note: God promises rains in season and land yielding produce for obedience; the sequence is exact, though it does not include the commentary's mutual plant growth or later violent loss.

basis: storehouse tithe; heavenly abundance
note: Bringing the tithe into God's storehouse is followed by promised abundance from heaven; it links the commentary's piled produce and due share with renewed provision.

basis: crop protected from destroyer
note: God promises to restrain the devourer so field fruit is not destroyed and the vine does not fail; it reverses the commentary's loss of a ripened crop after its due has been given.

basis: faithful speak one to another
note: Those who fear the Lord speak with one another and are heard and remembered; their reciprocal speech provides a human counterpart to the commentary's plants joining in a faithful group.

basis: produce worked for but not enjoyed
note: The commentary says a lifetime's yield can disappear; Micah names sowing without reaping, olives without oil, and grapes without wine, turning that loss into denied agricultural labor.

basis: sow without reaping; pressed crops lost
note: Micah threatens that the people will sow but not reap, tread olives yet lack oil, and crush grapes yet not drink wine; this is the commentary's lost harvest in a judgment on unjust gain.

basis: whirlwind and storm; clouds as dust
note: Nahum joins a divine whirlwind and tempest with clouds described as dust beneath God's feet; this puts the commentary's rain cloud and dust-raising whirlwind into one memorable storm image.

basis: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; withheld share causes lack
note: The proverb says one who withholds what ought to be given comes to lack; Hebrew מחסור from חסר connects the commentary's lost gain with its duty to give a crop's share, while cognacy remains unverified.

basis: one who waters is watered
note: The generous person prospers and the one who gives water receives water; the commentary's rain-fed, mutually joined plants become an ethical pattern of reciprocal support.

basis: poor person's crop swept away by injustice
note: The poor person's field can provide much food, yet injustice destroys it; the verse makes the commentary's harvest right and lost yield a social issue rather than mere weather.

basis: boasted gift; clouds without rain
note: A person boasting of a gift never given is likened to clouds and wind without rain; this applies the commentary's rain cloud to its nearby warning about showy giving whose benefit vanishes.

basis: one person sharpens another
note: The commentary interprets connected plants as people who counsel one another; Proverbs gives mutual sharpening as a concrete image of how one person forms another, though it does not use agricultural imagery.

basis: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; giver has no lack
note: The one giving to the poor will have no lack, but ignoring them draws curses; Hebrew מחסור gives an explicit inverse to the commentary's loss and its harvest-day obligation.

basis: full barns and overflowing vats
note: The commentary traces rain through crop to gathered produce; Proverbs depicts full barns and overflowing wine vats as the result of honoring God with firstfruits.

basis: full barns follow given firstfruits
note: The ensuing promise of barns filled with plenty turns the commentary's stacked grain into a yield linked to giving rather than showy or withheld charity.

basis: honor God with firstfruits
note: The commentary says the crop has a due on harvest day; Proverbs gives the first produce to honor God, making the yield a prescribed offering.

basis: firstfruits given from produce
note: The instruction to honor God from one's produce and firstfruits provides a concrete practice alongside the commentary's claim that a crop has a due share at harvest.

basis: tree beside water; fruit in season
note: The commentary pictures the exception to loss as plants joined in unbroken greenery; Psalm 1's planted tree bears fruit at its time and its leaf does not wither, giving that flourishing a righteous figure.

basis: watered tree bears seasonal fruit
note: The righteous are a tree planted by channels of water that gives fruit in season; the commentary likewise sees the exceptional faithful as greenery sustained by water and productive time.

basis: chaff driven by wind
note: The commentary's whirlwind lifts dust and its crop image ends in disappearance; Psalm 1 contrasts its fruiting tree with the wicked as wind-scattered chaff.

basis: wicked like windblown chaff
note: The wicked are chaff driven by wind, against the fruitful watered tree of the preceding verse; it precisely matches the commentary's contrast of lasting growth and works blown away.

basis: water from above satisfies earth
note: God waters mountains from above and earth is filled with the fruit of divine work; this supplies the commentary's downward rain and ensuing yield as one ordered provision.

basis: grass for cattle; plants for people
note: The commentary says pasture gives itself to the herd and describes grain as human yield; this verse pairs God-grown grass for cattle with plants for human use.

basis: grass for animals; plants for human food
note: Grass grows for livestock and cultivated plants provide human food; it directly joins the commentary's meadow for herds to the crop that becomes a community's provision.

basis: sown fields and planted vineyards yield fruit
note: People sow fields and plant vineyards that yield produce; the commentary's grain and vine garden likewise become the usable product of human labor on renewed land.

basis: blessed families and livestock multiply
note: The following blessing multiplies both people and livestock; it links the commentary's productive pasture to the vulnerable descendants whose future depends on a preserved yield.

basis: tears sown; joyful harvest
note: Sowing in tears ends in reaping with joy; the agricultural sequence gives patient difficulty before harvest the positive ending preserved by the commentary's exception.

basis: sowing in tears, reaping in joy
note: The commentary pairs steadfastness with the crop's rise and loss; this psalm makes a painful sowing issue in joyful reaping, adding a hope-filled harvest after hardship.

basis: cloud, rain, hill grass
note: God covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for the earth, and makes grass grow on hills; this gives the commentary's cloud-to-pasture transition in one verse.

basis: grass-fed animals receive food
note: The next verse says God gives food to animals; it connects the commentary's pasture given to herds to divine provision rather than vegetation alone.

basis: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; no lack
note: The shepherd's speaker says he lacks nothing; Hebrew אחסר marks provision as the inverse of the commentary's ruined yield, and the following pasture image makes that inverse concrete.

basis: חסר; lack (table sound correspondence only)
note: The commentary labels خسر as the loss of a harvest; the package lists חסר as a corresponding Hebrew root, and the shepherd-speaker says he will not lack, giving a concrete opposite outcome under care.

basis: green pasture and rest
note: The shepherd settles the speaker in green pastures beside quiet water; the commentary's meadow that gives itself to animals becomes a picture of sustained care.

basis: green pasture and still waters
note: The commentary describes pasture nourishing a herd; the shepherd here leads the speaker to green pasture and water, adding a personal image of provision that prevents want.

basis: صبر / צבר; table sound correspondence only; life's hoard
note: The passing human heaps up wealth without knowing who will gather it; צבר joins the commentary's stacked gain to the old-age question of what a life's product finally secures.

basis: watering furrows; soil softened for grain
note: The commentary begins with rain squeezed from clouds and later with crops; this psalm has God water the furrows and prepare grain, joining rainfall directly to yield.

basis: pastures with flocks; valleys with grain
note: The commentary connects rain-fed pasture and harvested grain; this verse places flocks in pasture and grain in valleys in one picture of a fruitful landscape.

basis: grain and human flourishing
note: Abundant grain covers the land while people flourish like field plants; the psalm turns the commentary's grain crop and joined green community into a linked vision of prosperity.

basis: raining upon cut grass
note: The hoped-for king comes like rain on mown grass and showers watering earth; it places restorative rain precisely after cutting, the positive answer to the commentary's lost harvest.

basis: tumbleweed and chaff before wind
note: The commentary describes a whirlwind lifting dust into a column; this verse makes enemies like rolling dust and wind-driven chaff, using airborne scattering as an image of defeat.

basis: fire consuming forest
note: The commentary's fiery cyclone burns a garden; this verse compares judgment on enemies to fire consuming a forest, extending the storm image to vegetation destroyed by flame.

basis: storm and tempest pursuing enemies
note: The commentary's إعصار is a destructive wind column; this verse calls for enemies to be pursued by storm and tempest, using violent weather as an image of reversal and judgment.

basis: truth sprouts from earth beneath righteousness
note: The psalm pictures truth springing from the earth while righteousness looks down from heaven; it gives the commentary's joined greenery and call to truth a striking common image.

basis: land gives its produce
note: The next verse promises the Lord's good gift and the land's yield; it supplies the harvest stage after truth springs from the ground in the preceding verse.

basis: old age and brief lifespan
note: The psalm reckons a human span as seventy or eighty years, full of trouble and swiftly gone; it adds the late-life horizon of the commentary's elderly garden owner to the nearby grass image.

basis: human generations swept away like grass
note: The psalm says God sweeps people away as grass renewing in the morning; it places the commentary's human loss inside the short life cycle of vegetation.

basis: morning bloom, evening wither
note: Grass blossoms in the morning and withers by evening; it closely parallels the commentary's quick turn from luxuriant growth to destroyed yield.

basis: fruit in old age; fresh and green
note: The commentary says a life's accumulated crop can be lost in its late years; this psalm instead says the righteous still bear fruit in old age, explicitly reversing that late-life outcome.

basis: fruit and green growth in old age
note: The righteous still bear fruit in old age and remain fresh and green; this is an exact positive alternative to the commentary's aged owner losing a mature garden just when dependents need it.

basis: storm clouds, showers, and field grass
note: The commentary links a rain cloud to pasture growth; Zechariah asks for rain from the maker of storm clouds, which gives showers and field grass.

basis: God gives rain and field plants
note: Those asking for spring rain receive showers and field plants; the verse carries the commentary's paired images of rain cloud and resulting greenery.

basis: vine fruit, land produce, heavenly dew
note: Zechariah's restored remnant receives a seed of peace, fruitful vine, productive ground, and heavenly dew; this unites the commentary's collective, watered garden, and tangible harvest.

basis: truth spoken to neighbors after restored harvest
note: After promising dew and yield to the remnant, Zechariah commands neighbors to speak truth and judge justly; this connects the commentary's green community to its mutual exhortation in truth.
